title: How to do high frequency/volume bench press without shoulder pain
summary: Growing the bench requires frequent, voluminous pressing, but high-frequency flat barbell benching causes shoulder overuse injuries in most lifters. He gives five ways to keep horizontal pressing volume high while sparing the shoulders (paused reps, dumbbell press, slingshot warm-ups, narrower grip, low-impact work like push-ups and flies) and an example week.

claims.claim: Flaring the elbows on horizontal presses puts more stress on the shoulder and eventually leads to injury.
An arch on the bench reduces range of motion so the shoulders stay in the pocket with less extension, keeping you injury-free longer.
High-volume, high-frequency benching leads to shoulder pain one way or another regardless of form, unless you are an outlier.
To progress on the bench, even for hypertrophy, most people must bench often; one weekly very high-volume session, or many low-rep sets in one session, doesn't work.
You also need enough volume per session; throwing in four sets of a press and calling it a day isn't enough.
Constant touch-and-go benching stresses the shoulder: the bounce/stretch at the bottom loads it, and form gets less strict when banging out reps.
Replace one bench day per week with a paused bench day: pause on the chest, on pins at chest level, or above the chest (Spoto press, pin press); pauses deload the shoulder.
He advises doing paused reps without pins so you keep control of the weight, a bodybuilder's preference.
Dumbbell bench press deloads the shoulder, but tuck the elbows rather than flaring them to shorten the range; do it the hard way to keep it healthy.
Slingshots do deload the bottom of the bench and are shoulder-friendly, but he believes slingshot strength doesn't carry over to the raw bench, while raw bench carries over to slingshot bench.
Slingshot bench becomes a skill in itself, depending on the slingshot's stiffness, and may change your form from regular bench.
Use submaximal slingshot bench to open a session as a warm-up, then follow with raw bench; it leaves you tight and warm and raw benching feels great.
A wider bench grip stresses the shoulders more; a narrower grip may move less weight but deloads the shoulder so you can do more pressing volume.

High-frequency, low-intensity movements (flies, cable flies, band flies, light semi-flies, push-ups) build pec hypertrophy and pressing volume without taxing the shoulder and help you be fresher for heavy days.
Push-ups every two days for very high volume are amazing for shoulder health and pec tendon health, provided you do them properly.
Example week: Monday close-grip bench, Wednesday main bench day, Friday football bar bench or paused/Spoto press, with push-ups between those days for frequency and volume.
This approach is aimed at hypertrophy; benching heavy only once a week may not be best for strength.
